text: the sun was warm and the sky was blue so we went down to the beach after lunch. my little brother ran into the water and a big wave knocked him over. he sat up and laughed with sand in his hair. we built a tall castle with a moat and watched the sea fill it up before we went home

our class has a pet fish called bob who lives in a tank near the window. every morning one of us feeds him a small pinch of food. bob swims to the top and eats it very fast. on friday we clean the glass and check the water is not too cold. bob is the best class pet we have ever had

the bus was late again so we stood at the stop and played a game. you have to name an animal that starts with the last letter of the one before. cat then tiger then rabbit then turtle. my friend said eel and i could not think of one that starts with l until the bus came and i said lion

on the weekend my dad and i made pancakes for the whole family. we mixed the flour and eggs and milk in a big bowl. the first one stuck to the pan and broke into bits so we ate it. the rest came out round and gold. we put lemon and sugar on top and ate them all while they were hot

at the park there is a long slide and a rope swing near the creek. we like to see who can swing out the highest. my cousin is the bravest and holds on with one hand. we stay until the sun goes down and the birds get loud in the trees. then we walk home and talk about what we will do next time

it rained all day so we could not go out at lunch. we sat in the library and read comics and played cards. the rain made a loud noise on the roof and the windows were all fogged up. when the bell rang the sun came out and there was a big puddle on the oval that everyone tried to jump over

Koalas spend most of the day asleep in the forks of gum trees. They eat only eucalyptus leaves, which are tough and give them very little energy. To save that energy, a koala can sleep for up to twenty hours a day. When it is awake, it uses its sharp claws and strong arms to climb from branch to branch looking for the freshest leaves.

Our science class built a model volcano out of clay and an old plastic bottle. We poured baking soda into the bottle and added a few drops of red food colouring. When we tipped in the vinegar, foam shot out of the top and ran down the sides. Everyone cheered, but the teacher reminded us to wipe the table before the bell.

The first people to live in Australia arrived more than sixty thousand years ago. They knew how to find water in the desert, which plants were safe to eat, and how to read the stars at night. Many of these stories and skills have been passed down from older people to younger people for thousands of years, and they are still shared today.

Every year our school runs a sports day at the local oval. Each house has its own colour, and students paint their faces and bring flags. There are running races, a long jump pit, and a tug of war that everyone wants to win. Even the teachers join in for the final relay, although most of them are much slower than they think they are.

Learning to type properly takes practice, just like learning to play an instrument. At first it feels slow to keep your fingers on the home row, and you may want to look down at the keys. If you keep going for a few minutes each day, your fingers start to remember where each letter is, and your speed will slowly climb.

The museum trip was the best excursion of the year. We saw the skeleton of a giant wombat that lived long ago, and a meteorite that had fallen in the outback. In the last room there was a robot that could draw your face. It took about two minutes, and the picture looked a lot more like a potato than a person.

Volcanoes form where melted rock, called magma, pushes up through cracks in the Earth's crust. When the pressure becomes too great, the volcano erupts, sending lava, ash and gas into the air. Some eruptions are gentle, with rivers of glowing lava; others are explosive and can be heard thousands of kilometres away. Scientists, known as volcanologists, study the ground's movements to predict when the next eruption might happen.

In 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon. Millions of people around the world watched on black-and-white televisions, including many in Australia, where a radio telescope at Parkes helped to send the pictures to Earth. The astronauts collected rocks, planted a flag and left footprints that, without any wind to blow them away, are probably still there today.

Plastic rubbish is one of the biggest problems facing our oceans. Bottles, bags and tiny pieces called microplastics are carried by rivers and wind until they reach the sea. Turtles often mistake floating bags for jellyfish, while seabirds feed small fragments to their chicks. Reducing single-use plastic, recycling carefully and joining beach clean-ups are simple ways that everyone can help.

The Great Barrier Reef stretches for more than 2,300 kilometres along the coast of Queensland. It is made up of thousands of individual reefs, built over centuries by tiny animals called coral polyps. The reef is home to an extraordinary variety of life, including turtles, sharks, dugongs and more than 1,500 species of fish. Unfortunately, warmer ocean temperatures are causing coral bleaching, which threatens the entire ecosystem.

Computers store every piece of information as binary, a system that uses only two digits: 0 and 1. Each digit is called a bit, and eight bits together make a byte. A single letter typed on a keyboard usually takes one byte to store, while a high-quality photograph might need several million. Programmers write instructions that tell the computer exactly how to process all of these numbers.

Bush fires are a natural part of the Australian landscape, but they can be extremely dangerous. Hot, dry weather and strong winds allow flames to spread quickly through grass and trees. Some native plants, such as banksias, actually need the heat of a fire to release their seeds. Firefighters, many of whom are volunteers, work tirelessly to protect homes, wildlife and entire communities.
